subject: Geography
title: Structure of Earth and Types of Rocks
learningOutcomes: Define geography and describe its three branches — physical, human and environmental geography.
Describe the three layers of the Earth (crust, mantle and core) and their thickness, state and temperature.
Explain the Continental Drift Theory, Pangaea and how sea floor spreading supports it.
Compare continental and oceanic plates and explain convergent, divergent and transform plate movements.
Identify the plates and mountain ranges of Pakistan and classify the three main types of rocks.

sections.heading: What Is Geography?
sections.body: Geography is the study of the Earth, its land and the people living on it — the word comes from the Greek 'geo' (the Earth) and 'graphein' (to write). It has three branches. Physical geography studies natural features and covers relief and drainage (the height and shape of the land, and water bodies like rivers and lakes), weather and climate, and natural vegetation and soil. Human geography studies people and their activities — population, settlement and economic activity. Environmental geography studies how human activities such as mining and industry affect nature, causing pollution and climate change.

sections.heading: Interior of the Earth
sections.body: Scientists study the Earth's interior by examining how earthquake waves travel through it, and drilling has shown that it gets hotter with depth. The Earth has three layers. The crust is the thin, rigid outer layer (5–60 km) broken into plates. The mantle below it is about 2,000 km thick, made of semi-solid rock at around 1,000°C, where convection currents flow and move the plates. The core has two parts: a liquid outer core (about 2,250 km thick, ~4,400°C, made of liquid nickel and iron) and a solid inner core (about 1,250 km thick, over 5,430°C, made of solid iron). The inner core stays solid despite being the hottest layer because it is under enormous pressure.

sections.heading: Pangaea and Continental Drift
sections.body: Millions of years ago all the Earth's land was joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea, which slowly broke apart into today's continents. Alfred Wegener proposed this Continental Drift Theory in 1912. It gained acceptance after scientists discovered the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain range where magma (molten rock) rises and cools to form new crust. This sea floor spreading pushes the ocean floor — and the continents — apart.

sections.heading: Crustal Plates and Their Movement
sections.body: The crust is broken into roughly 20 tectonic plates that carry the continents. Continental plates are made of land — lighter, thicker and less dense (feldspar and aluminium) — so they rest higher on the mantle; oceanic plates form the seabed and are denser and thinner (basalt and magnesium). Plates move in three ways. Convergent (collide): two continental plates fold into fold mountains, while an oceanic plate subducts under a continental one, forming an oceanic trench — a destructive boundary. Divergent (move apart): magma rises to form new crust and ridges — a constructive boundary. Transform (slide past): a fault line forms — a passive boundary.

sections.heading: Crustal Plates in Pakistan
sections.body: Pakistan lies at the boundary of two continental plates, the Indian Plate and the Eurasian Plate. Because both are the same density, their collision caused folding that formed the Himalayan fold mountains, and the convergent movement continues today, so the Himalayas grow a little each year. At Jaglot in Gilgit Baltistan, three great ranges — the Himalayas, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush — meet, and the Gilgit and Indus Rivers join at a confluence.

sections.heading: Rocks, Minerals and the Rock Cycle
sections.body: A rock is a naturally formed, non-living material made of mineral grains; minerals (like quartz and feldspar) are natural solids with a crystal structure; and elements (like gold or carbon) are the simplest substances that cannot be broken down. There are three types of rock. Igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens (granite, basalt, gabbro). Sedimentary rock forms when weathering and erosion break down and transport particles that are compacted into layers, sometimes with fossils (limestone, sandstone). Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change existing rocks — limestone becomes marble and granite becomes gneiss, which is found in Pakistan's Kaghan valley.

definitions.definition: The height and shape of the land, such as mountains, plateaus and plains.
The condition of the atmosphere at any given time (it changes daily).
The average weather of a place recorded over many years (usually 30+ years).
The thin, rigid outermost layer of the Earth (5–60 km) broken into plates.
Circular movements of heat in the mantle that make the plates move.
Alfred Wegener's 1912 theory that the continents were once joined as Pangaea and have drifted apart.
When a denser oceanic plate is forced beneath a continental plate into the mantle.
Rock formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.
Rock formed by the weathering, erosion and compaction of particles in layers.
Rock formed when existing rocks are changed by great heat and pressure.

examTips: Learn the Earth's layers in order — crust, mantle, outer core, inner core — and remember the inner core is the hottest yet solid because of enormous pressure.
Match each plate movement to its boundary: convergent = destructive, divergent = constructive, transform = passive.
Fold mountains (Himalayas) come from two continental plates colliding; subduction and an oceanic trench (Andes, Peru-Chile Trench) come from an oceanic plate meeting a continental one.
Learn one example for each rock type: igneous = granite, sedimentary = limestone, metamorphic = marble (from limestone) and gneiss (from granite).
